{"id": "12:48/q04", "question": "How did Joseph recognize the first severe year?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "12:48/q04/p1", "position": "A man who had previously left part of his food ate his whole allotment, showing Joseph that the famine had begun.", "reasons": "Ibn Zayd says the man ordinarily saved half his portion. Zayd ibn Aslam, as reported by al-Māwardī, al-Ṭabrisī and al-Qurṭubī, says Joseph served food for two; the accounts vary in whether this is described as eating an entire or double portion."}]}
{"id": "12:48/q05", "question": "How do the dream's cows and ears relate to these years?", "turns_on": "Whether the dream images primarily signify successive kinds of years or also prescribe the planting and preservation measures needed during them.", "positions": [{"id": "12:48/q05/p1", "position": "The lean cows and dry ears signify barren years, and their eating the fat cows depicts famine consuming stores from prosperous years.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī, Ibn Kathīr and al-Biqāʿī identify the lean cows and dry ears with drought; al-Biqāʿī cites the dream imagery in 12:36 and 12:43. Ibn ʿĀshūr maps cows to agricultural years, fatness to fertility, leanness to drought, ears to provisions, and seven dry ears to stores accumulated over seven years. Al-Bayḍāwī says the figurative eating follows the dream symbol. Al-Bursawī clarifies that thin cows did not literally eat fat ones. Qatāda says the first seven fertile and next seven dry years are indicated by the dream. Al-Qummī's report recounts the king's cows and ears and Joseph's interpretation."}, {"id": "12:48/q05/p2", "position": "The cows picture yearly provisions and the ears picture the grain and the work needed to preserve it.", "reasons": "Ṭabāṭabāʾī takes fat cows as abundant harvests from repeated planting and lean cows as shortages eating saved food. For him green ears are stores and dry ears point to keeping grain unthreshed; the lean cows' failure to eat every fat cow allows a remaining reserve."}]}
{"id": "12:48/q06", "question": "Is Joseph's explanation a forecast, practical direction, or both?", "turns_on": "How much of Joseph's statement is read as decoding the dream's future and how much as instructions to meet that future.", "positions": [{"id": "12:48/q06/p1", "position": "It forecasts seven fertile years followed by seven barren years and a further recovery year.", "reasons": "Qatāda says the first fourteen years are shown by the dream and the later abundant year was separately disclosed. The Study Quran describes an ensuing fifteen-year agricultural cycle. Al-Qummī reports Joseph interpreting plentiful years, famine years and then rain. Ṭabāṭabāʾī explicitly objects to treating the dream as merely this forecast."}, {"id": "12:48/q06/p2", "position": "It sets out the practical policy of repeated cultivation, storage and rationing needed to survive famine.", "reasons": "Ṭabāṭabāʾī favors this as the dream's force for the king; planting repeatedly, preserving grain in ears and rationing reserves are required measures, and the symbols depict that work. Ibn ʿAṭiyya says Joseph's storage plan carries the population through drought, including use of scant produce grown during famine. The Study Quran says the first harvests should be stored for food in the second phase."}, {"id": "12:48/q06/p3", "position": "Joseph's reply combines interpretation of meaning, practical advice and disclosure of the unseen further year.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān identifies these three kinds of speech and says the interpretation is by meaning rather than the dream's exact wording."}]}
{"id": "12:48/q07", "question": "How did Joseph know the further abundant year?", "turns_on": "Whether Joseph's knowledge of the unasked-for year in 12:49 came from earlier divine teaching or a direct disclosure at this time.", "positions": [{"id": "12:48/q07/p1", "position": "He used knowledge God had previously taught him.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī reports this as one side of the exegetes' disagreement over Joseph's interpretation."}, {"id": "12:48/q07/p2", "position": "He learned it through direct revelation.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī says the prediction of an abundant year not asked about in the dream supports direct revelation; Qatāda, reported by al-Rāzī, says God granted Joseph knowledge of that additional year, while the preceding fourteen years are indicated by the dream."}]}
{"id": "12:48/q08", "question": "Why are the years said to eat the stored food?", "turns_on": "Whether 'eating' is explained through inhabitants' action, the verb's sense of exhausting, or a developed image of predatory years.", "positions": [{"id": "12:48/q08/p1", "position": "Eating is attributed figuratively to the years because their inhabitants eat during them.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī and al-Thaʿlabī cite poetry calling day heedless and night asleep for people's acts; al-Wāḥidī and Ibn al-Jawzī also cite a sleeping night. Al-Zamakhsharī describes a figurative grammatical subject. Ibn ʿAṭiyya calls it metonymy and cites 27:86, 10:67 and 40:61; al-Samīn cites the day in 10:67. Al-Bayḍāwī says the attribution also matches the dream. Al-Ālūsī says it expresses what people undergo; Ibn ʿĀshūr locates the loss in the years as its time. Abū Ḥayyān compares describing a day as seeing. Al-Baghawī calls it an expansive metaphor."}, {"id": "12:48/q08/p2", "position": "'Eat' means use up, exhaust or destroy the stored food.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Anbārī, reported by al-Wāḥidī, and al-Ṭabrisī cite the Arab idiom that a journey ate a camel's flesh; al-Wāḥidī also cites a line by Dhū al-Rumma. Al-Ālūsī reports this explanation from some commentators. Ibn ʿĀshūr cites Q 4:2 for consumption, while still calling attribution to years rational metaphor. Ibn ʿAṭiyya says drought may be described as consuming and drying vegetation. Al-Dāmghānī specifies that the hard years' eating consumes the stored harvest completely."}, {"id": "12:48/q08/p3", "position": "The wording personifies the harsh years as ravenous predators attacking people and their provisions.", "reasons": "Ṭabāṭabāʾī relates this image to the sense of shidād as attacking things and the following description of devouring."}]}
{"id": "12:48/q09", "question": "What variant reading is reported for 'they eat'?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "12:48/q09/p1", "position": "Al-Sulamī reads yaʾkulūn, 'they eat,' in the masculine plural, referring to people.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān reports al-Sulamī's third-person reading and says it speaks of people eating rather than addressing the listeners."}]}
{"id": "12:48/q10", "question": "What is the food 'put forward for them'?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "12:48/q10/p1", "position": "It is the harvest and provisions gathered and stored in the fertile years for consumption in the coming famine.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ glosses it as crops prepared in advance. Al-Ṭabarī, Qatāda, al-Māwardī, Ibn Kathīr and others specify earlier stores. Ibn ʿAṭiyya includes even scant produce obtained during famine in what sustains the people. Al-Bursawī says grain was stored in its ears. Ibn Kathīr says drought sowing yields no return, which makes the prior stores necessary. Al-Iṣlāḥī says the drought destroys the stores and leaves very little."}]}
{"id": "12:48/q11", "question": "Why does the verse say 'for them' of the years?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "12:48/q11/p1", "position": "The pronoun reinforces the personification of the years or corresponds to the dream's imagery.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī offers both explanations for lahunna."}]}
{"id": "12:48/q12", "question": "What is the little amount excepted from consumption, and what is it for?", "turns_on": "Whether the exception identifies an unspecified protected remainder, seed needed for later planting, or a little withdrawn from stores for present eating.", "positions": [{"id": "12:48/q12/p1", "position": "A small part of the harvest remains protected in storage as a reserve.", "reasons": "Maqātil, al-Ṭabarī, Ibn ʿAbbās, Qatāda and others gloss the exception as the little saved or secured. Al-Māwardī reports protected storehouses. Al-Nasafī says the people keep only a small part of what they save. Al-Rāzī describes it as a protected remnant, although his wording says only a little of the reserves will be consumed. Ibn ʿĀshūr says the exception urges ample stockpiling."}, {"id": "12:48/q12/p2", "position": "The little preserved is seed for sowing after the famine, protecting the next harvest.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī calls reserving seed a further possibility. Al-Baghawī, al-Qurṭubī, al-Bayḍāwī, al-Bursawī, al-Ālūsī and Kur'an Yolu give this purpose. Ṭabāṭabāʾī says it is both a reserve and seed for the recovery year, and reasons from the dream's lean cows not eating every last fat cow."}, {"id": "12:48/q12/p3", "position": "A small amount is kept outside storage for current consumption while the reserve lasts through the famine.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī distinguishes the long-lasting reserve from a little taken out for consumption."}]}
{"id": "12:48/q13", "question": "What does tuḥṣinūn mean?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "12:48/q13/p1", "position": "It means to protect, secure, save or store provisions.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba, Ibn ʿAbbās, Qatāda, Abū ʿUbayda and other exegetes give these close glosses. Al-Ṭabarī, al-Wāḥidī, al-Ṭabrisī, Abū Ḥayyān and al-Ālūsī explain iḥṣān through a protected place, enclosure or fortress. Al-Māwardī specifies protected storehouses. Al-Qurṭubī notes that Abū ʿUbayda's different wording has the same meaning. Al-Suddī's wording is to raise or save the remainder."}]}
{"id": "12:48/q14", "question": "How is qalīlan parsed?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "12:48/q14/p1", "position": "It is accusative as the exception.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī gives this grammatical analysis."}]}

{"id": "12:48/q16", "question": "What farming and storage measures carry people through famine?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "12:48/q16/p1", "position": "Cultivate repeatedly, keep much of the good harvest in storage, protect grain in its ears, and ration it through the drought while retaining seed.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya says successive harvests and even meager famine produce support the people. {"id": "12:48/q17", "question": "Does the passage permit storing food until it is needed?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "12:48/q17/p1", "position": "Yes, storing food for a later need is permissible.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī derives this ruling from the passage's instruction to save grain."}]}
{"id": "12:48/q18", "question": "What does the king's dream show about an unbeliever's dream?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "12:48/q18/p1", "position": "An unbeliever's dream can be true and interpreted as seen, especially where a believer is concerned; this dream also served as a messenger's sign and miracle.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī draws these points from the king's dream and its fulfillment."}]}
{"id": "12:48/q19", "question": "What happened in the reported famine economy under Joseph?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "12:48/q19/p1", "position": "Joseph stockpiled harvests and sold food successively for money, valuables, livestock, servants, property, land and finally people's freedom; afterward he freed them and restored their possessions and kingship.", "reasons": "Ṭabāṭabāʾī transmits this from al-Riḍā and says he omits many similar economic reports because most do not directly help interpret these verses."}]}
{"id": "12:48/q20", "question": "What comparison is reported between this famine and Quraysh's hardship?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "12:48/q20/p1", "position": "The Prophet prayed that Quraysh suffer seven years like Joseph's famine; hardship began but ended before seven years.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya reports the comparison and the shorter duration."}]}
{"id": "12:48/q21", "question": "What happened after the seven famine years, and how is the following year's wording read?", "turns_on": "The reported reading specifies rain, rather than rescue, as the sense of the following year's wording.", "positions": [{"id": "12:48/q21/p1", "position": "The following year brought rain and renewed plenty.", "reasons": "Al-Qummī's report says Joseph predicted rain after the plentiful and famine years. Al-Ṣādiq explains the following year's yughāth by rain rather than rescue; al-ʿAyyāshī transmits the same explanation. Al-Wāḥidī and Qatāda refer to the further abundant year beyond the dream's fourteen years."}, {"id": "12:48/q21/p2", "position": "Al-Ṣādiq reads the following year's verb passively as 'they are rained upon.'", "reasons": "Ṭabāṭabāʾī reports al-Ṣādiq's passive reading and its transmission by al-ʿAyyāshī."}]}
{"id": "12:48/q22", "question": "What broader point does Joseph's story illustrate?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "12:48/q22/p1", "position": "God directs human affairs in ways people cannot foresee; they may hate what benefits them or love what harms them.", "reasons": "Asad contrasts this Qur'anic theme with the romantic account of Joseph in Genesis and cites Q 2:216."}]}

{"id": "12:48/q24", "question": "What is the grammatical function of mā in the two clauses?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "12:48/q24/p1", "position": "Both occurrences are relative mā, referring to what was prepared for the hard years and what is stored.", "reasons": "Al-Burhān lists both clauses among examples of relative mā. {"id": "12:49/q01", "question": "What does ذَٰلِكَ refer to?", "turns_on": "Whether the demonstrative resumes the numbered years, whose grammatical form can take masculine agreement, or the drought itself.", "positions": [{"id": "12:49/q01/p1", "position": "The seven preceding years.", "reasons": "Al-Kalbī explains the masculine demonstrative by the form of سبع, which lacks a feminine marker; Ibn al-Qāsim gives the same grammatical account, and al-Kalbī cites a parallel verse in which masculine agreement follows such a feminine noun (al-Wāḥidī; Ibn al-Jawzī)."}, {"id": "12:49/q01/p2", "position": "The drought.", "reasons": "Muqātil identifies the antecedent as the drought rather than the years (al-Wāḥidī; Ibn al-Jawzī)."}]}
{"id": "12:49/q02", "question": "What does the choice of عَامٌ convey?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "12:49/q02/p1", "position": "It marks a full twelve-month year of relief under God's control.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī says the word designates a complete twelve months and underscores that God alone knows and controls the coming relief."}, {"id": "12:49/q02/p2", "position": "It suggests ease and fertility after the hard years.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī contrasts عام, often associated with ease and fertility, with سنة, often associated with hardship and famine; both mean year."}]}
{"id": "12:49/q03", "question": "How did Joseph know the details of the year after the famine?", "turns_on": "Whether the dream or the normal end of drought establishes only general relief, or also establishes the precise rain, produce, and timing promised here.", "positions": [{"id": "12:49/q03/p1", "position": "God disclosed an additional, unasked-for year to Joseph by revelation or prophetic knowledge.", "reasons": "Muqātil, al-Ṭabarī, al-Thaʿlabī, al-Ṭabrisī, al-Qurṭubī, al-Bursawī, al-Manār as quoted by al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī, and Kuranyolu say it was outside the king's dream; Qatāda says God taught Joseph the unasked year (ʿAbd al-Razzāq, al-Ṭabarī, al-Thaʿlabī, al-Wāḥidī, Ibn al-Jawzī, al-Rāzī, al-Qurṭubī, Abū Ḥayyān, al-Durr). Al-Ṭabarī and al-Ṭabrisī call it a sign of prophethood and truthfulness; al-Qurṭubī calls it evidence of merit. Al-Wāḥidī uses the detailed forecast to support direct revelation over taught interpretation; al-Kashshāf and al-Rāzī distinguish the general end of famine from the precise rain and pressing, which require revelation. Abū Ḥayyān distinguishes interpretation, practical advice, and an unseen report; al-Ālūsī treats revelation as apparent. Ibn ʿAbbās says Joseph volunteered the rain and pressing details (al-Durr)."}, {"id": "12:49/q03/p2", "position": "The dream or the end of the seven hard years itself implied a return to abundance.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya says the dream's interpretation already implied that hardship ends after seven years (reported by Abū Ḥayyān). Al-Bayḍāwī allows inference from the end of drought or God's customary relief after hardship, as well as revelation; the dream's cows and ears symbolize the fertile and famine years and consumed stores (also al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī quoting him). Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī derives the final year from the repeated seven and the end of the need to manage sowing and reserves. Al-Ālūsī rejects a merely natural inference as too vague for the specific promised relief."}]}
{"id": "12:49/q04", "question": "What does يُغَاثُ ٱلنَّاسُ mean?", "turns_on": "The rain derivation from ghayth, the relief derivation from ghawth, or abundance as the practical form of aid; the following pressing clause and the forms of the Arabic roots are cited.", "positions": [{"id": "12:49/q04/p1", "position": "People receive rain.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba equates ghayth with rain; Ibn al-Sikkīt describes rain falling on the land (al-Wāḥidī; al-Rāzī). Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, and Qatāda are cited for rain (al-Ṭabarī, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, al-Māwardī, Ibn ʿAṭiyya, al-Ṭabrisī, Ibn al-Jawzī, Abū Ḥayyān, al-Durr, al-Ālūsī). Al-Qurṭubī distinguishes forms for rain, help, and seeking aid; Abū Ḥayyān and al-Samīn call the rain derivation triliteral, and al-Samīn quotes a Bedouin woman's غثنا for obtaining rain. Al-Tabāṭabāʾī prefers rain because pressing follows; he says Nile floods depend on rain upstream in Sudan and cites Lisān al-ʿArab for ghayth as vegetation grown from rainwater. Asad likewise notes Egypt's Nile floods depend on upstream rain. Al-Ṣādiq takes the word from rain in reports collected by al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī; al-Ṭabrisī says ghayth is needed rain. Al-Sāmarrāʾī contrasts Qurʾanic ghayth, beneficial rain, with amṭara used for punitive rain; he cites 42:28 for mercy after despair and 12:49 for relief and harvest, against punitive-rain examples in 27:58, 26:173, 7:84, and 25:40."}, {"id": "12:49/q04/p2", "position": "God relieves and rescues people from famine and distress.", "reasons": "Al-Thaʿlabī and Ibn ʿAṭiyya connect the word with g

hawth, aid or relief; al-Ṭabrisī defines it as urgently needed help that removes harm. Al-Iṣlāḥī prefers help as the literal force and says drought drives people to plead before rain comes; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī finds rain more apt in this context, except under a passive rain reading of the next verb."}, {"id": "12:49/q04/p3", "position": "People receive abundant produce.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĪsā gives this as an explanation in al-Māwardī; Ibn al-Jawzī attributes relief through abundance to al-Māwardī."}]}
{"id": "12:49/q05", "question": "How is يَعْصِرُونَ read?", "turns_on": "The subject or addressee, active versus passive vocalization, and whether the verb denotes pressing, deliverance, or rain; al-Ṭabarī weighs established regional transmission against a reported rain reading.", "positions": [{"id": "12:49/q05/p1", "position": "Active third-person yaʿṣirūn: they press.", "reasons": "Ibn Mujāhid, al-Fārisī, Ibn ʿAṭiyya, Ibn al-Jawzī and others assign yāʾ to Ibn Kathīr, Nāfiʿ, Abū ʿAmr, ʿĀṣim, and Ibn ʿĀmir; it resumes الناس (Ibn Khālawayh, al-Fārisī, al-Ṭabrisī, al-Samīn). Al-Ṭabarī accepts it as an established regional reading equal in meaning to the address form; Qiraat-Er calls it standard active Form IV. ʿAlī is reported to object to active pressing of wine and direct the reciter toward rain (al-Ṭabrisī; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī). Ibn al-Jazarī says the readers other than Ḥamza, al-Kisāʾī, and Khalaf use third-person narration."}, {"id": "12:49/q05/p2", "position": "Active second-person taʿṣirūn: you press.", "reasons": "Ḥamza and al-Kisāʾī read tāʾ, according to Ibn Mujāhid, al-Fārisī, al-Thaʿlabī, and others; it addresses Joseph's questioners and continues the earlier direct address, including قدمتم (al-Fārisī, al-Jishumī, al-Baghawī). Ibn Khālawayh says it singles them out; al-Ṭabrisī says it may include others. Al-Ṭabarī accepts this established reading too, and Ibn ʿAbbās is reported with a second-person form tied to milking (al-Durr). Ibn al-Jazarī includes Khalaf alongside Ḥamza and al-Kisāʾī among those who read the verb as direct address."}, {"id": "12:49/q05/p3", "position": "Passive third-person yuʿṣarūn: they are relieved or rained upon.", "reasons": "Al-Aʿraj, Jaʿfar b. Muḥammad, and ʿĪsā are named by Ibn Jinnī, Ibn ʿAṭiyya, al-Ṭabrisī, Abū Ḥayyān, al-Samīn, and al-Ālūsī. Some explain rescue; others rain from rain-bearing clouds in 78:14 (Ibn Abī Ḥātim, al-Thaʿlabī, al-Māwardī, al-Zajjāj, Ibn al-Jawzī, al-Rāzī, al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī). Saʿīd b. Al-Ṭabarī rejects a non-established yāʾ rain reading against the regional readers."}, {"id": "12:49/q05/p4", "position": "Passive second-person taʿṣarūn: you are rescued or rained upon.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān reports a second reading from ʿĪsā meaning rescue; al-Samīn and al-Ālūsī also assign him a passive address form. Al-Qurṭubī reports ʿĪsā's tāʾ with open ṣād for rain, alongside a kasra variant of the same sense; al-Durr mentions a second-person reciter and 78:14."}, {"id": "12:49/q05/p5", "position": "An intensified or assimilated form is read.", "reasons": "Al-Naqqāsh transmits a doubled form, described as intensive by Abū Ḥayyān, al-Samīn, and al-Ālūsī; their descriptions vary as to vocalization and passive form. Zayd b. ʿAlī reads a form from taʿtaṣirūn with assimilation, which may mean squeezing or rescue (Abū Ḥayyān, al-Samīn, al-Ālūsī). Al-Naqqāsh also records a reading about squeezing moisture (Ibn ʿAṭiyya)."}]}
{"id": "12:49/q06", "question": "What do people do in يَعْصِرُونَ?", "turns_on": "Whether the verb is physical squeezing, a related action such as milking, an Arabic rescue or prosperity idiom, or a rain expression; cited readings, poetry, and early authorities supply the competing evidence.", "positions": [{"id": "12:49/q06/p1", "position": "They press fruit and plants for juice or oil.", "reasons": "The lists vary: grapes, olives, sesame, other fruit, sugarcane, radish, oil, wine, syrup, or water (Ibn ʿAbbās, Qatāda, Mujāhid, Ibn Jurayj and many commentators). Al-Qurṭubī cites al-Bukhārī for Ibn ʿAbbās; al-Wāḥidī relates sesame oil, grape wine, and olive oil and points to 12:36. Al-Fārisī and al-Ṭabrisī report fourteen years without pressing oil or grapes; Ibn ʿAṭiyya and Abū Ḥayyān report that nothing was pressed during drought. Al-Samīn calls this the clearest sense; al-Biqāʿī says pressing expresses the transition to fertility. Al-Ṭabarī rejects the rescue derivation because Companion and Successor interpretation favors pressing; al-Wāḥidī reports al-Fārisī favoring both pressing and rescue. {"id": "12:49/q07", "question": "Why mention pressing produce in the promised year?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "12:49/q07/p1", "position": "Pressing marks an exceptional return of fertility and specific crops after famine.", "reasons": "Al-Fārisī and al-Ṭabrisī report that no oil or grapes had been pressed for fourteen years; Ibn ʿAṭiyya and Abū Ḥayyān say nothing was pressed during drought. {"id": "12:49/q09", "question": "Why shift from direct address to ٱلنَّاسُ and يَعْصِرُونَ?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "12:49/q09/p1", "position": "The wider phrasing signals that people can again live without managing famine reserves.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī contrasts Joseph's earlier direct address to the group with his reference here to people receiving rain or aid and pressing produce."}, {"id": "12:49/q09/p2", "position": "The third-person verb resumes الناس; the second-person reading addresses Joseph's petitioners.", "reasons": "Ibn Khālawayh, al-Fārisī, al-Jishumī, al-Baghawī, al-Ṭabrisī, al-Samīn, and Qiraat-Er explain the pronouns this way; al-Ṭabrisī says the address can include others."}]}
{"id": "12:49/q10", "question": "How does the promised year relate to the king's dream and Joseph's interpretation?", "turns_on": "Whether the earlier seven fertile years are dream symbols being decoded, or Joseph's agricultural policy in response to a foreseen famine.", "positions": [{"id": "12:49/q10/p1", "position": "It is an additional year after seven fertile and seven famine years.", "reasons": "Qatāda calls it an unasked-for eighth year after the fourteen years (ʿAbd al-Razzāq, al-Ṭabarī, al-Rāzī, Abū Ḥayyān). Fat cows and green ears signify fertile years; lean cows and dry ears signify famine, and stored abundance is consumed (al-Bayḍāwī, al-Nasafī, al-Bursawī, Ibn ʿĀshūr). Study Quran counts fifteen years in the interpretation. Al-Qummī's report likewise has plenty, famine, then rain."}, {"id": "12:49/q10/p2", "position": "Joseph gave a survival policy for the expected famine, rather than deriving the fertile years from the dream.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī rejects commentators' claim that the dream forecasts seven fertile followed by seven barren years; he reads Joseph's directions as the necessary policy for surviving anticipated famine."}]}
{"id": "12:49/q11", "question": "Why does Joseph end with this good news?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "12:49/q11/p1", "position": "The placement brings hope after a discouraging forecast and shows Joseph's excellence.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says relief after hardship comforts the hearers; al-Ālūsī contrasts the placement with Joseph's answer to the prisoners, where prediction came first, and says the final glad news highlights his excellence."}]}
{"id": "12:49/q12", "question": "What inward state does the year of relief signify?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "12:49/q12/p1", "position": "The soul enjoys fruition after complete tranquility and security.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī reads the year of relief and pressing as the soul's enjoyment after attaining security."}]}
{"id": "12:49/q13", "question": "What happened to Egyptian people and property during Joseph's famine administration?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "12:49/q13/p1", "position": "Joseph sold stored food for successive classes of property, then freed people and restored their possessions.", "reasons": "A report from al-Riḍā says the sequence was money, valuables, livestock, servants, property, land, then personal freedom; Joseph later freed Egyptians and restored possessions and kingship. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says he omits many similar economic reports because they do not directly explain these verses."}]}
{"id": "12:49/q14", "question": "How did Joseph recognize the famine's first day?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "12:49/q14/p1", "position": "A man ate both of two food portions Joseph prepared for him.", "reasons": "Zayd b. Aslam's report, quoted by al-Ālūsī, says Joseph called that the first day of the hard years."}]}
{"id": "12:49/q15", "question": "Does the counselors' dismissal of the dream challenge the rule that a dream follows its first interpretation?", "turns_on": "Whether calling a dream meaningless is an interpretation, and whether the rule applies to dreams with several admissible meanings.", "positions": [{"id": "12:49/q15/p1", "position": "The dismissal challenges that rule.", "reasons": "Al-Balkhī argues that the counselors called the king's vision confused dreams, yet that assessment did not determine its outcome (reported by al-Ālūsī)."}, {"id": "12:49/q15/p2", "position": "A dismissal as meaningless may not count as an interpretation.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī replies with the hadith that a dream hangs on a bird's wing until interpreted, and says the counselors' words may not have been an interpretation."}, {"id": "12:49/q15/p3", "position": "The rule applies to dreams with several possible meanings, once one interpretation is made.", "reasons": "Ibn al-ʿArabī gives this restriction, reported by al-Ālūsī."}]}
{"id": "12:49/q16", "question": "What does the king's dream show about true dreams and their interpretation?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "12:49/q16/p1", "position": "An unbeliever can have a true dream.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī reports this use of the passage; he also finds some associated claims opaque, including advice against seeking interpretation at sunrise, sunset, or night and a claim that a sleeping dream interprets itself."}, {"id": "12:49/q16/p2", "position": "Dreams should be interpreted by qualified people.", "reasons": "Kuranyolu draws this lesson from Joseph's disclosed forecast and cites 12:4–6."}]}
{"id": "12:49/q17", "question": "What does the account teach about God's direction of events?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "12:49/q17/p1", "position": "God directs events beyond human understanding, including things people wrongly desire or dislike.", "reasons": "Asad contrasts the Qur'anic account with the Genesis account of Joseph's fortunes and invokes 2:216."}]}
{"id": "12:49/q18", "question": "How do people respond to severe hardship in the promised relief?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "12:49/q18/p1", "position": "They cry to God for help until their pleas are answered.", "reasons": "Al-Iṣlāḥī treats asking for aid as the word's literal force and says drought exposes its full effects; even extreme polytheists and disbelievers forget their imagined deities and call on the one God, as the Qur'an says."}]}
{"id": "12:49/q19", "question": "What did Joseph's guidance through the drought accomplish?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "12:49/q19/p1", "position": "It earned admiration from the king and ordinary Egyptians.", "reasons": "Al-Iṣlāḥī says Joseph's management of the drought won broad admiration."}]}
{"id": "12:49/q20", "question": "Who are ٱلنَّاسُ in the promised year?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "12:49/q20/p1", "position": "The people of Noah's ark, in Noah's time after Adam.", "reasons": "Al-Dāmghānī groups the people mentioned in 12:49 with the people of Noah's ark and specifies Noah's time after Adam."}, {"id": "12:49/q20/p2", "position": "The people of Egypt.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzī says the people in Joseph's appeal to return to them (12:50) and in this promise are Egyptians."}]}
{"id": "12:49/q21", "question": "What do qataʿ and sakt mean in the takbīr transition?", "turns_on": "Whether earlier writers used sakt loosely for an ordinary stop or in its technical sense.", "positions": [{"id": "12:49/q21/p1", "position": "An ordinary pause, without grammatical ending or a technical breathless sakt.", "reasons": "The author of al-Nashr attributes this practice to al-Mahdawī, Makkī, Abū al-ʿIzz, Abū al-ʿAlāʾ, and many others; he rejects al-Jaʿbarī's technical reading as a misunderstanding of their usage."}, {"id": "12:49/q21/p2", "position": "Qataʿ is a technical breathless sakt.", "reasons": "Al-Jaʿbarī alone interprets it this way, as reported and rejected by the author of al-Nashr."}]}
{"id": "12:49/q22", "question": "How is the root of يَعْصِرُونَ used across Qur'anic passages?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "12:49/q22/p1", "position": "Its forms connect the pressing in Joseph with al-ʿAṣr, rain-bearing clouds, and the whirlwind in al-Baqara.", "reasons": "Bint al-Shāṭiʾ notes that this form is unique in the Qur'an and cites the root in Joseph's dream and harvest year (12:36, 12:49), al-ʿAṣr (103:1), and the whirlwind (2:266), alongside 78:15–16; she derives the forms from pressure that extracts juice, clouds' water, or wind-driven clouds."}]}
{"id": "14:34/q01", "question": "What does God giving from all people asked mean?", "turns_on": "Whether asking is verbal or implicit, whether كل is literal or abundant, and whether من limits the gifts.", "positions": [{"id": "14:34/q01/p1", "position": "God grants a portion or some kinds of what people ask, according to their benefit and His wisdom.", "reasons": "Al-Akhfash and al-Tabari supply an omitted 'thing' and cite 27:23; Tabari prefers this common reading. Abu al-Hasan and al-Akhfash's extra min permits totality."}, {"id": "14:34/q01/p3", "position": "God gives unasked gifts as well as asked gifts, or gifts never asked for.", "reasons": "Muqatil cites mercy; al-Dahhak names sun, moon, night and day, and says some gifts were not imagined. Al-Akhfash and Jish

{"id": "14:34/q02", "question": "How does من كل ما سألتموه work grammatically?", "turns_on": "Whether من is partitive or extra, and what object is omitted.", "positions": [{"id": "14:34/q02/p1", "position": "من is partitive, and an object such as 'thing' or 'portion' is understood.", "reasons": "Al-Akhfash and Tabari compare 27:23; Abu Ali compares 2:61 and 27:16. Ibn Atiyya requires a supplied second object. Samin attributes this analysis to Sibawayh; al-Alusi explains that كل still spans the kinds."}, {"id": "14:34/q02/p2", "position": "من is extra in an affirmative clause; every requested thing is the second object.", "reasons": "Abu al-Hasan analyzes the prepositional phrase as accusative; Samin reports this from al-Akhfash. Qurtubi records the resulting complete-grant sense."}, {"id": "14:34/q02/p3", "position": "كل is an expansive expression for many kinds, not exhaustive totality.", "reasons": "Al-Akhfash compares everyday 'knows everything'; Tabari and others cite 6:44, the opening of every door. {"id": "14:34/q03", "question": "How is من كل read?", "turns_on": "The standard genitive annexation contrasts with tanwīn; on tanwīn, mā may be relative or negative.", "positions": [{"id": "14:34/q03/p1", "position": "The common reading attaches كل to ما without tanwīn.", "reasons": "Al-Tabari prefers the authoritative reciters' agreement and rejects the alternative; Ibn Jinni says the object is an understood share of each kind. Jishumi and Thalabi identify it as the common reading."}, {"id": "14:34/q03/p2", "position": "A reported reading puts tanwīn on كل; its sense varies with the parsing of ما.", "reasons": "Abu Salih contrasts it with the reading without min; Ibn Jinni lists Ibn Abbas, Hasan, Dahhak, Muhammad and Jafar ibn Ali, Amr ibn Fa'id and Yaqub. Other lists add Salam, Qatada and Nafi. It can mean requested gifts, need by condition, or unasked gifts."}]}
{"id": "14:34/q04", "question": "What can ما and the pronoun in سألتموه denote?", "turns_on": "Relative, descriptive, infinitival, and negative readings assign different functions and pronoun references.", "positions": [{"id": "14:34/q04/p1", "position": "ما is relative or descriptive, referring to what was requested or needed.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya, Samin and al-Alusi allow a relative; Samin prefers it on the tanwīn reading as second object. Abu Hayyan objects to some proposed restored resumptive pronouns, while al-Alusi reports a defense."}, {"id": "14:34/q04/p2", "position": "ما is infinitival, with the suffix pronoun referring to God.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya, Abu Hayyan and Samin say the verbal noun stands for the request or requested thing; Samin distinguishes the pronoun's referent from the relative or descriptive analysis."}, {"id": "14:34/q04/p3", "position": "On the tanwīn reading, ما is negative and the phrase is circumstantial: gifts came without asking.", "reasons": "Al-Dahhak's account is widely transmitted; al-Zamakhshari gives it, while Abu Hayyan says it clashes with the common annexed reading and Samin prefers relative mā for harmony."}]}
{"id": "14:34/q05", "question": "Why can a person's request go unanswered?", "turns_on": "Whether the limitation lies in benefit, the petitioner's knowledge, or the distinction between species and individual requests.", "positions": [{"id": "14:34/q05/p1", "position": "God grants only what is beneficial, at its right time, and may avert harmful requests.", "reasons": "Jishumi invokes partitive من, distinguishes the informed petitioner, and Tabrisi names harm to religion or another person. Asad appeals to ultimate divine wisdom; the Study Quran reports a Prophetic account of grant now, stored reward, or equivalent evil averted, excluding sin and severed kinship."}, {"id": "14:34/q05/p2", "position": "The species' genuine intrinsic requests are met, while individual verbal prayers may be insincere or misdirected.", "reasons": "Tabataba'i cites 2:186 and distinguishes all beings' dependence from explicit verbal requests."}]}
{"id": "14:34/q06", "question": "What is the reading of وآتاكم?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "14:34/q06/p1", "position": "A reading has أتاكم in place of آتاكم.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathir records the variant without further argument."}]}
{"id": "14:34/q07", "question": "What does نعمة الله mean, and why is it singular?", "turns_on": "Whether the singular is a verbal noun substitute or a collective noun for bestowed things.", "positions": [{"id": "14:34/q07/p1", "position": "It is a noun standing for the verbal noun إنعام, God's act of bestowal.", "reasons": "Al-Wahidi says a verbal noun need not be pluralized; Razi, Tabrisi, Abu Hayyan and Alusi transmit this analysis."}, {"id": "14:34/q07/p2", "position": "It means the bestowed blessings collectively; a singular construct or generic noun covers them all.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan and Alusi prefer this over the verbal-noun view. Baydawi and Bursawi point to construct definiteness; Tabataba'i calls it the whole genus; Samin says the bestowed thing."}, {"id": "14:34/q07/p3", "position": "Blessing means anything agreeable, including conditions for benefit and harms warded off.", "reasons": "Alusi says this lexical sense is wider than the religious technical sense of a result praised in the end; it admits continuing existence and absent impediments."}]}
{"id": "14:34/q08", "question": "Why can God's blessings not be enumerated?", "turns_on": "Whether the point is sheer number, hidden detail within each gift, inability to preserve them, or inability to repay them.", "positions": [{"id": "14:34/q08/p1", "position": "Their number and the detail within even one favor exceed human counting and knowledge.", "reasons": "Tabrisi, Qurtubi and Ibn Atiyya name senses, bodily form, health, provision, creation and guidance; Qushayri adds protection from trials. Razi traces bread through seasons, elements, weather, iron, tools, anatomy and medicine, and nerves through every branch and organ; Alusi repeats these examples and argues that conditions, continuing existence and averted afflictions are unbounded. Baydawi distinguishes kinds from instances. Ibn Ashur notes overlooked breath, digestion and circulation. Tustari and Sulami name Muhammad as a surpassing blessing. Abu al-Darda warns against reducing favors to food and drink."}, {"id": "14:34/q08/p2", "position": "People cannot fulfill gratitude for favors, since thanking is itself a further favor.", "reasons": "Talq calls for repentance morning and evening; Ibn Kathir transmits David's admission, Shafi'i's recursive gratitude, and a poem that every limb's praise falls short. Qushayri and Sulami stress unending obligation. Al-Sajjad calls acknowledging inability itself gratitude; Sulayman al-Taymi says God asks thanks according to capacity."}, {"id": "14:34/q08/p3", "position": "They cannot all be preserved or remembered.", "reasons": "Al-Kalbi gives the memory sense; Ibn al-Jawzi cites 18:49 and 58:6 for exhaustive recording. Ibn Ashur observes that even known blessings are forgotten."}, {"id": "14:34/q08/p4", "position": "They cannot be endured, performed, or managed in full.", "reasons": "Al-Farra compares 73:20 on keeping night-vigil times; others construe that verse as inability to bear it. Ibn al-Jawzi reports Muqatil's night-prayer capacity sense."}]}
{"id": "14:34/q09", "question": "What does إحصاء mean here and what is its origin?", "turns_on": "Counting, encompassing, recording, and capacity are reported senses.", "positions": [{"id": "14:34/q09/p1", "position": "It means counting accurately, originally with pebbles, and by extension encompassing a total.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzi gives counting as fundamental, cites 72:28 for knowledge, and folds it into counting. Alusi cites al-A'sha's pebbles line and reports a rival account of pebbles marking bundles; al-Raghib favors the older pebble-counting account. Ibn Ashur says pebbles once fixed large totals without error."}, {"id": "14:34/q09/p2", "position": "In other Qur'anic uses it can mean exhaustive preservation, recording, or capacity.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzi cites 18:49 and 58:6 for preserving, 36:12 and 78:29 for written record, and 73:20 for capacity; al-Wahidi also compares 73:20."}]}
{"id": "14:34/q10", "question": "Why use a conditional when failure to count is certain?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "14:34/q10/p1", "position": "The conditional addresses the human impression that counting might be possible.", "reasons": "Alusi says the details of even one blessing defeat the attempt."}]}

{"id": "14:34/q12", "question": "What do ظلوم and كفار say about a person?", "turns_on": "Whether the wrong is directed at self, God, blessings, or gratitude's rightful recipient, and whether hardship and ease distinguish the traits.", "positions": [{"id": "14:34/q12/p1", "position": "A person wrongs himself by disobeying or withholding thanks, and denies or misuses God's favors.", "reasons": "Muqatil links sins and failure to worship; Tabari adds redirecting worship. Alusi describes self-imposed deprivation."}, {"id": "14:34/q12/p2", "position": "The injustice is complaint or despair in hardship; ingratitude is hoarding and withholding in prosperity.", "reasons": "Thalabi, Jishumi, Kashshaf, Razi, Baydawi, Nasafi, Abu Hayyan and Alusi transmit the contrast."}, {"id": "14:34/q12/p3", "position": "Injustice misdirects gratitude to someone other than the benefactor; ingratitude denies the benefactor.", "reasons": "Thalabi and Baghawi distinguish misplaced thanks from denial; Jishumi names attribution to another originator; Islahi glosses kaffar as thanking someone else."}, {"id": "14:34/q12/p4", "position": "Inwardly, a person ruins innate preparedness by turning to perishing nature and is veiled from grace.", "reasons": "Qashani and Bursawi describe the loss of potential; Sulami and Alusi add the error of imagining human gratitude can repay God."}]}
{"id": "14:34/q13", "question": "Why does the verse close with human injustice and ingratitude?", "turns_on": "Whether the clause explains failed gratitude, the preceding rebuke, or the infinity of favors.", "positions": [{"id": "14:34/q13/p1", "position": "It explains why humans fail to honor favors and reinforces the earlier rebuke of exchanging blessings for disbelief.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan connects 14:28–30 and setting up rivals; Samin concurs. He reports that al-Burhan likewise contrasts Ibrahim's concern with human nature against al-Nahl's establishment of God's divinity and attributes."}, {"id": "14:34/q13/p2", "position": "It underscores the abundance of blessings and the human inability to thank or notice them.", "reasons": "Razi says people tire, forget and overlook other favors while reflecting on some; Tabataba'i links the explanation to heedlessness."}]}
{"id": "14:34/q14", "question": "How does this ending relate to the ending of 16:18?", "turns_on": "Whether the two endings describe recipient and giver in their contexts, or one replaces the other.", "positions": [{"id": "14:34/q14/p1", "position": "Here the recipient's injustice is foregrounded, while 16:18 names God's forgiveness and mercy as giver.", "reasons": "Razi, Abu Hayyan, Ibn al-Munir, Samin, Biqai and Itqan contrast human failure with continuing divine generosity; Ibrahim follows disbelief and rivals, while al-Nahl details favors, divine attributes and the postponement of punishment. Samarrai points specifically to the blessings and divine attributes in 16:5–15 and says each sura's surrounding cadence suits its distinct ending. He also reports Ma'tarak al-Aqran's recipient-versus-Benefactor explanation and al-Burhan's contrast between human nature in Ibrahim and divine attributes in al-Nahl."}, {"id": "14:34/q14/p2", "position": "The Ibrahim ending was abrogated by the al-Nahl ending.", "reasons": "Ibn Zayd's claim is transmitted by al-Sakhawi; Abu Hayyan dismisses it, and Alusi says it deserves no attention."}]}
